title: Projected Climate Change Impacts on Deep‐Sea Corals of the Red Sea
content:
Through modeling the distribution of four taxonomically diverse deep-sea coral taxa under present and future climate conditions, we identify potential biodiversity hotspots of deep-sea corals in the Red Sea, providing important considerations for international, long-term management of these natural marine resources.


ABSTRACT

Ocean warming, acidification, and deoxygenation, among other co-occurring factors, are shifting species ranges throughout the marine environment. Mesophotic and deep corals are understudied in their response to climate changes, particularly in the Red Sea, which has relatively high temperatures and salinities and is projected to undergo major changes in the future, with little assessment of the impacts to date. Ecological niche modelling can be used to explain the known distribution of a species, predict its current range, and estimate future range shift under changing ocean scenarios. Here, we estimate the area of suitable habitat for four mesophotic and deep-sea corals (Acanthogorgia spp., Stylaster tritoni, Bathypathes thermophila, and Madracis interjecta) across the whole Red Sea under present conditions and under different scenarios of future environmental changes (years 2090–2100). We found variations in the responses of these corals, but two of the four taxa are projected to lose significant amounts of their current habitats, while the other two lose a smaller portion. In particular, the scleractinian coral M. interjecta is likely to lose the largest proportion of its habitat, while the black coral B. thermophila may experience the least change. Deeper areas may become suitable for these corals, but colonisation will depend on their ability to disperse. We also assessed the potential biodiversity hotspots both now and in the future, finding the northern Red Sea to be one ecologically important area. These results enable marine spatial planning in support of an effective long-term conservation action to protect these important habitats.
